curated.title: The AI & LLM Systems Engineering Handbook
curated.subtitle: From Zero to Production: Build, Evaluate, and Operate Language-Model Systems

parts.title: How a Model Learns
description: If you can read code, you already have the habit this part depends on: you want to see the mechanism run. A language model is an enormous table of numbers and one procedure for nudging them, and that procedure works the same way on a problem small enough to check by hand.

So we start with a straight line and finish with a language model you train yourself, one that reads characters and writes more of them. You pick up the mathematics the rest of the book leans on at the moment it earns its place, then size up the machine that runs it. You need no machine-learning background, and everything here is here because a later chapter leans on it or a real training run will test it.

parts.title: Models, Messages, and Measurement
description: A language model turns text into a row of probabilities, one token at a time. Follow that path closely, and surprising answers start to have causes you can find and settings you can choose on purpose.

We go from the pieces of a sentence to a complete Transformer, then on to decoding, chat formats, and measurement. By the end, when a fluent answer comes back, you will know how to test whether it did the job.

parts.title: Evidence and Grounded Answers
description: An application's facts usually live in documents that change on their own schedule, and the model knows none of them. A useful answer depends on those facts surviving a long trip: from a file to a record, from a record to a search result, and from a search result into the words of a response.

This part follows that trip through extraction, chunking, search, and evaluation, with permissions traveling alongside the text. Each stage gives you a place to find out where an answer went wrong, and the last question is always the same: is this answer supported, and was this reader allowed to see what supports it?

parts.title: Learning from Examples and Preferences
description: Your evaluation just told you what the model gets wrong. Now you have to teach it better, and every way of teaching has its own way of fooling you.

We start with reviewed examples and follow them through training, floating-point arithmetic, adapters, and preference learning, then attack the result. One question keeps coming back: when a number improves, did the behavior you wanted improve with it?

parts.title: Agents That Can Act and Recover
description: A model can propose a useful next step, and your application stays responsible for what actually happens. Turning that proposal into a dependable workflow takes clear inputs, real observations, permissions, and rules for when to stop.

These chapters build that control around a working loop. We look at how context shapes a decision, how untrusted text reaches the model, and how a person reviews one exact action. The last chapter follows an interrupted operation far enough to decide how it can safely continue.

parts.title: Serving Under Real Workloads
description: A model that works in a notebook still has to work at nine in the morning, when everyone shows up at once. Serving is where latency, memory, and cost become one problem, and where a correct decision can still arrive too late.

We follow one request from the first wait to the last token, then widen out: the memory it holds, the work it can reuse, the scheduler it competes in, the bits its weights are stored in. From there we watch it in production, ship new versions safely, run a fleet through a morning surge, and finish by earning the benchmark number all of that depended on.

parts.title: A Governed Support System
description: Everything so far has been a mechanism. Now it has to work for a person with a problem, under a budget, with someone accountable when it goes wrong. A faster answer can cost more, a routing change can quietly change what the answer is based on, and a slow review can leave a customer waiting.

This last part puts the pieces together. We decide who owns the risks, turn a cost target into something a gateway can enforce, and then follow one customer's duplicate charge from the first message to the final record. By the end, you will have followed one ticket through the agent, retrieval, gateway, and review layers you built, and you'll be able to say why it ended the way it did.

reference.subtitle: Language Models, Evaluation, Training, Agents, and High-Throughput Serving

parts.title: Language Models, Evaluation & Applications
description: A model can sound sure and still be wrong about the document in front of you. Look at the text it actually received, the representations it built, and a check that tells you whether the answer is usable.

With that, you can put together tools, retrieval, safety checks, a record of what happened, and a release decision you would explain to a teammate. The later chapters on model internals and serving are easier once you know what the system is for.

parts.title: Transformer Architectures & Attention
description: When an application depends on a model, a bad token often comes from inside the forward pass. The model may have skipped a position, hidden the wrong context, or flattened the scores before decoding.

Stay with one representation as it moves through embeddings, attention, images, position, and normalization, until it becomes the next token. When you later change training, you should know which step moved the prediction.

parts.title: Pretraining, Fine-Tuning & Alignment
description: A model that is almost right is a good reason to teach it something more specific. You want an example that would change the behavior, and a test that would show the change is real.

The chapters here are that plan: data, a small model you can inspect, precision, distributed training, adapters, preferences, rewards you can check, distillation, and merging. Each one changes behavior and leaves you a way to test the result.

parts.title: Autonomous Agents, Tool Protocols & Sandboxing
description: Giving a model a tool is the easy part. The satisfying work is deciding what you trust in the result. The model can suggest a step. Your runtime decides what may run, what may be remembered, and when a person should look.

These chapters take retrieval and tool use into larger indexes and longer jobs: access control, structured output, execution limits, human review, memory, and recovery. The model's words stay a suggestion.

parts.title: High-Throughput Inference & Serving Systems
description: A good answer that shows up late is a different product from the one you had in mind. Once many people arrive together, memory, batching, and scheduling are part of how the product feels.

Follow one request into the serving engine. KV state, parallelism, kernels, precision, and decoding are how you get to capacity, recovery after a failure, and quality you can still measure after launch.

parts.title: System Design & Production Codebases
description: A chapter can be right on its own and still cause trouble beside the rest of the system. Serving changes the latency budget. Retrieval changes what the model may claim. Training changes which failures you can see.

The last chapters put those pieces into full designs, then follow the same choices through real training and inference code. You will have pinned source and measurements to lean on, including the place where the design stops holding.

parts.title: Foundations of AI Systems & Applied Mathematics
description: The work gets more interesting once your workspace gives the same answer twice, and once you can see why a number moved. Start with a reproducible setup, tensors, probability, and a small network you train yourself.
Take that into language modeling, prompting, and a small application. When a prediction surprises you, you should be able to name the earlier idea that explains it.

parts.title: Classical Machine Learning & Production ML Systems
description: Fitting the rows you trained on is a good start. What you want next is a decent guess on a new row, and a way to notice when the data, the split, or the metric led you astray.

These chapters fit simple models, check whether they travel to new rows, and build the path around them: data quality, experiments, training loops, features, and monitoring. Later language-model work uses the same habits.
